title: Gallery Ceiling Sensors
story: An art gallery is fitting motion sensors to a ceiling of n × n panels. Each sensor beams along its row, its column and both diagonals to the walls, and two sensors on one beam set each other off. Some panels are glass skylights: nothing mounts on glass, but beams pass through it. The gallery needs exactly n sensors and wants to know how many layouts are possible.
task: Write countLayouts(ceiling). ceiling is a list of n strings of length n; ceiling[r][c] is '.' for a normal panel and '#' for a skylight. Return the number of ways to place n sensors on normal panels so that no two share a row, a column or a diagonal.
Two layouts are different if some panel has a sensor in one and not in the other. Skylights do not block beams. If no layout exists, return 0.
constraints: Every row of ceiling has length n.

examples.explanation: Writing each row's sensor column, the two layouts are 1, 3, 0, 2 and its mirror image 2, 0, 3, 1. Every other try shares a column or diagonal.
The skylight at row 0, column 1 rules out 1, 3, 0, 2, which needs a sensor there. The mirror 2, 0, 3, 1 survives.
The only panel is a skylight, so no sensor can be placed and the answer is 0.

hints: On a 4 × 4 ceiling with 4 sensors, how many sensors can one row hold? So how many does each row get?
Exactly one sensor per row, so pick a column for row 0, then row 1, and so on. A column is allowed only if the panel is not glass and no placed sensor watches it.

A sensor at (r, c) watches column c, the diagonal where row − col = r − c, and the one where row + col = r + c. Keep three boolean lists (columns, row − col, row + col) so each check is instant. Shift row − col by n − 1 so it is never negative.

Write count(row): if row == n, return 1. Otherwise sum count(row + 1) over every allowed column, marking the column and both diagonals before the call and clearing them after. A row with no allowed panel returns 0 and the search backs up.
bruteForce: Choosing any n of the n² panels means about 17 trillion choices on a 10 × 10 ceiling. Even one sensor per row and column (every column ordering) is 10! = 3,628,800 full layouts, each checked at the end, though most clash within the first two or three rows.

js: * @return {number} how many valid layouts of n sensors

tests.note: a column of skylights: every column needs a sensor, so no layout
a full row of skylights: no layout

js: const downUsed = new Array(2 * n - 1).fill(false); // same row - col
const upUsed = new Array(2 * n - 1).fill(false);   // same row + col
if (row === n) return 1; // one sensor in every row
const d = row - col + n - 1, u = row + col;

walkthrough: Each row holds exactly one sensor, so you only choose a column per row. A panel's diagonals are identified by row − col and row + col, so "is this panel watched?" is three lookups.
Trace the open 4 × 4 ceiling, writing the chosen columns so far:

• Put row 0's sensor in column 0. Row 1 can then use column 2 or 3. With 0, 2, all of row 2 is watched: dead end. With 0, 3, row 2 takes column 1, then all of row 3 is watched: dead end. So column 0 gives 0 layouts.
• Put row 0's sensor in column 1. Row 1 can then only use column 3, row 2 only column 0, and row 3 only column 2, so this gives 1 layout.
• Column 2 mirrors column 1 and gives 1 layout, and column 3 mirrors column 0 and gives 0.

The total is 2. A common bug is checking only one diagonal direction, which on the open 4 × 4 ceiling would also count the layout 3, 2, 1, 0, where all sensors sit on one diagonal. Another is forgetting to clear the marks after the recursive call, so later branches see sensors that are no longer there.
solution.timeWhy: Row r has at most n − r free columns, so there are at most n! paths, and the column and diagonal checks cut most of them off within a few rows.
solution.spaceWhy: Three boolean lists of size at most 2n − 1, and a recursion depth of n.
solution.takeaway: For placement puzzles, find the structure that forces one choice per step (here, one sensor per row), and keep a small set of 'already taken' markers so each candidate is checked in O(1). Mark before recursing, unmark after.
